problemText: Which of the following is a research question rather than a topic?
choices: A broad subject area that covers many different aspects of footwear and physical performance.
A specific type of athletic shoe worn by soccer players on the field.
An examination of how sports equipment has changed throughout the years.
How do different types of soccer cleats affect a player's running speed on wet grass?
hints: A research question is a complete sentence that ends with a question mark.
A topic is just a word or phrase with no way to know when you are finished.

problemText: Jamal is writing a short research report about butterflies. He starts with the question, 'How many species of butterflies exist in the world?' His teacher asks him to test his question against the three standards for a good research question. Which standard does Jamal's question fail?
choices: Broad enough — the question has only one true answer sitting in one place, not needing multiple sources.
Narrow enough — the question covers so many different butterfly species and geographic regions that it would require research across numerous unrelated topics.
Answerable by evidence — the question requires readers to make personal judgments about what counts as beautiful or important in nature.
All three standards — the question lacks a question mark and is written as a statement rather than an inquiry.
hints: A single fact in one location is not a research project; it is just a lookup.
Think about whether this question would need you to gather pieces from several different sources or just find one number.

problemText: Sofia wants to research whether peanut butter is a healthy food. She writes the question, 'Is peanut butter a healthy food?' What is the main problem with Sofia's research question?
choices: It is too narrow in scope because it limits her research to only one specific food item rather than examining an entire food group.
It asks for a judgment rather than asking what evidence can show — different people could read the same facts and disagree.
It is answerable by evidence in a measurable way because sources provide clear nutritional data that settles the question completely.
It is too broad because the term peanut butter includes many varieties and preparations that would each require separate research.
hints: Some questions have a question mark but still cannot be settled by sources because they ask what someone prefers or judges to be good.
Think about whether 'healthy' can be measured by evidence or whether different people might have different opinions about it.

problemText: Hassan is researching skateboarding and starts with the topic 'Skateboard Tricks.' He then narrows his topic by asking, 'Why do some skateboard tricks require more balance than others?' After searching, he finds that several websites and instructional videos each address different reasons balance matters in tricks. However, he realizes that most of his sources answer the entire question in just one or two pages. What should Hassan do to his research question?
choices: Stop researching immediately because he has already found sufficient information to complete his entire project.
Make his question more specific by asking only about the balance requirements of a single skateboard trick and eliminating comparisons.
Widen his question by adding another layer of complexity, such as asking how balance training methods differ for different tricks.
Reformulate his question to ask for his own personal opinion about which tricks are the most difficult to perform.
hints: If one or two sources already answer your whole question, the question was too narrow and needs to be widened back out.
Refocusing means adjusting your question as you search — if it is too small, add another limit or layer to make it need more sources.

problemText: Maya is writing a three-page report about rain forests. She develops the question, 'How do the types of plants found in tropical rain forests compare to the types of plants found in temperate forests in terms of the way they receive sunlight?' After finding five detailed sources that each discuss sunlight and plant adaptation in different forest types, Maya realizes her sources contain enough information to answer this question fully. According to the lesson, what does this tell Maya about her research question?
choices: Her question is too narrow because it can be answered using evidence from multiple reliable sources without going beyond what she needs.
Her question is still too broad because it should focus on only one specific forest ecosystem rather than comparing two different types.
Her question is too vague because it uses the word 'compare' instead of asking whether something is true or false in a yes-or-no format.
Her question is likely at the right level — it needed multiple sources to answer and is not so large that it could fill an entire book.
hints: A good research question needs more than one source but is small enough to actually finish in the space you have.
The fact that her five sources together provide enough information to answer the question suggests it was sized right for this project.

problemText: Carlos is researching social media and starts with a broad question: 'How does social media affect teenagers?' He narrows it by asking, 'How do social media platforms affect teenagers' sleep patterns?' He finds six sources on this topic, and together they provide enough material for a five-page report. However, as he reads more carefully, Carlos notices that his sources discuss sleep patterns in teenagers aged thirteen to nineteen, but also mention that sleep effects differ significantly for younger children aged eight to twelve. Carlos realizes his original narrowed question did not specify an age group. What does this situation demonstrate about the research process?
choices: Carlos's question was actually too broad, and he should refocus it by adding an age limit based on what his sources revealed.
Carlos made a mistake in his original question and should have predicted the age-difference issue before he started searching.
Carlos should ignore the information about younger children and pretend his sources only discuss teenagers.
Carlos needs to start over completely because his original question is now ruined by the discovery of age differences.
hints: Refocusing your question as you search, and even narrowing it further after you find what sources actually contain, is part of doing the research, not a sign of failure.
When your sources show you that your question needs another limit to be truly clear, adding that limit is the normal way research questions improve.

problemText: You are researching whether after-school sports improve students' grades. What does it mean for a source to be credible when answering this question?
choices: The source was written by someone named, has a way to know the information firsthand, and you understand why they wrote it.
The source has an official-looking website with professional colors and a serious tone, so it appears trustworthy to readers.
The source is the first result when you search for the topic online, meaning search engines ranked it highest.
The source uses lots of statistics and numbers to support its claims, even if you cannot verify where those numbers came from.
hints: Think about the three questions you ask about every source.
Design and appearance are not the same as credibility.

problemText: You find two sources about how many students ride the school bus at Fernbrook Middle. Source 1 is a post on a social media page that says, 'I think most kids here take the bus,' signed by an unknown account. Source 2 is a report on the school district's website, written by the transportation coordinator, with exact counts from the bus roster. Which source is more credible for this question, and why?
choices: Source 1, because it comes from a student who attends the school and experiences the bus system daily.
Source 2, because the transportation coordinator keeps the actual bus records and is named.
Source 1, because social media posts reach more people and represent common opinions held at the school.
Source 2, because it was published on an official website rather than on a social media platform.
hints: Ask yourself who wrote each source and how they would actually know.
Firsthand access to records beats a guess, even from someone inside the school.

problemText: Your research question is: did the new school lunch menu actually reduce food waste? You find a blog post written by a parent who visits the cafeteria once a week and says the trash bins look emptier now. You also find the school's official food-waste report, written by the cafeteria manager, showing the actual weight of food waste measured on a scale before and after the menu change. Which source gives you better evidence for your research question, and what is the main reason?
choices: The parent's blog, because parents have a long history of observing school cafeterias and noticing changes over time.
The parent's blog, because it was written by someone who personally cares about reducing waste in the school.
The cafeteria manager's report, because it is based on what was actually measured and counted, not on how something looked.
The cafeteria manager's report, because managers have official titles and therefore their reports must always be more accurate than parent observations.
hints: Think about how each person would know their information.
A guess about how something looks is not the same as a measured record.

problemText: Your class is researching whether a new bike lane on Maple Street made biking safer. You find three sources. Source A is a comment on the town Facebook page from 'CyclingFan47' (no real name given) saying, 'The new lane is great and way safer.' Source B is a report by the town police department's safety officer listing the number of bike accidents on Maple Street before and after the bike lane was built. Source C is a promotional flyer from BikeCo, a bicycle shop on Maple Street, claiming 'Our bike sales have doubled since the lane opened, which proves it made biking way safer.' Using the three credibility questions, which source or sources would you trust most for this question, and why?
choices: Sources A and C together, because both people are excited about the bike lane, have personal investment in it, and would benefit if more people believe it is safer.
Source B only, because the police officer is named, has direct access to accident records, and has no financial reason to exaggerate the safety gain.
Source C only, because the bike shop owner works right there on Maple Street, observes riders daily, and can speak from firsthand experience about how behavior has changed.
All three equally, because each one provides a different perspective on the bike lane, all three come from people with community ties, and together they offer a complete picture.
hints: For each source, ask who wrote it, how would they know, and what would they gain.
When motives conflict with access to records, the one with actual measurements usually matters more.

problemText: Two sources disagree about how much plastic the school's recycling program actually collects. Source X, from the school facilities manager (who measures the weight on a scale monthly), reports 120 pounds a week. Source Y, from an environmental club flyer, claims recycling 'probably around 300 pounds a week to really help the planet.' The facilities manager does not work for the environmental club and has no reason to hide good numbers. Running the three credibility questions on each source, what does this disagreement tell you?
choices: The disagreement is itself a clue to check how each person knows their number; Source X is more likely to be correct because the facilities manager has direct access to actual weights, while Source Y offers no explanation for how they arrived at 300 pounds.
The disagreement proves that one source must be using a different method of measurement, so you should average the two numbers together to get the most accurate estimate of actual collection.
The disagreement means you cannot determine which number is correct without knowing whether the school's recycling happens every day or just once a week.
The disagreement shows that both groups care about recycling but have estimated differently, so the real number is probably somewhere between 120 and 300 pounds per week.
hints: When sources disagree, run the three questions on each one and compare the answers.
The source with actual, firsthand records usually outweighs the one with a guess or an estimate.

problemText: Your research question is: does the town's new water-conservation program actually save water? You find Source 1: a post by the town mayor on the town website saying the program is 'hugely successful,' but no numbers are given. You find Source 2: a peer-reviewed article by a hydrologist (water scientist) at a university, describing a detailed study of three similar towns over two years, two of which adopted the conservation program and one that did not; the towns with the program used about 15 percent less water on average. You find Source 3: a newsletter from SaveWater Inc., a company that sells water-saving equipment, claiming the program 'cuts water use by up to 50 percent' but offering no details about how they measured this. All three sources are named, but you need to decide which to rely on. Using all three credibility questions plus the idea that disagreement between sources is itself a clue, explain which source or sources give you the strongest evidence and why.
choices: Source 1 is strongest because the mayor holds an elected office and would damage their reputation if they made false claims about a major town program to the public.

Source 2 is strongest because the hydrologist studied multiple towns over time with no financial stake in the outcome, while Source 3 sells equipment and has a motive to exaggerate, and Source 1 gives no measured numbers at all.

Source 3 is strongest because it claims the biggest improvement, represents a company with expertise in water-saving technology, and has likely tested the program more thoroughly than the town itself.

All three are equally credible because they all come from named sources with relevant positions, each one mentions different measurements, and considering all three perspectives together gives the fullest understanding.
hints: Notice what each source gains if readers believe it: does someone make money, win an argument, or just report findings?
When one source has firsthand data from multiple years and towns, and another sells a product related to the claim, the disagreement points to which one to trust.

problemText: Which of these is the main difference between a quote and a paraphrase? A quote uses a source's exact words and a paraphrase does not. But what else separates them?
choices: A paraphrase is shorter than a quote because it leaves out less important details.
A paraphrase rebuilds the idea in new words and a new sentence structure, while a quote copies the exact wording letter for letter.
A paraphrase always requires a source name, but a quote does not need one.
A paraphrase is used when the wording itself is the point, and a quote is used when only the general idea matters.
hints: Think about what 'rebuild' means — does the sentence structure stay the same or change completely?
The lesson says a paraphrase covers about as much ground as the original sentence, so length is not what makes them different.

problemText: You are writing about how plants grow, and your science textbook states: 'Plants need sunlight, water, and nutrients from soil to grow strong.' You want to use this information but not copy the exact words. Which sentence is a real paraphrase, not a word swap?
choices: Plants require sunshine, moisture, and minerals from earth to grow strong.
Plants need sunlight, water, and nutrients from soil to grow strong, according to the science textbook.
For a plant to become strong and healthy, it must receive sunlight and water and also draw nutrients from the soil.
Soil nutrients, water, and sunlight are what plants need for strong growth.
hints: A real paraphrase rearranges the whole idea and lets it take a new shape — which choice does not keep the original sentence order?
Look for the choice where the main parts of the sentence sit in different slots than they do in the original.

problemText: A website about ocean animals says: 'Dolphins use echolocation to find food in the water.' You write the sentence below in your report. Is this a correct quote, a correct paraphrase, or a plagiarism mistake? 'Dolphins use echolocation to find food in the water.' (Your report gives no quotation marks and does not name the website.)
choices: It is a correct quote because you copied the words exactly and they are from a reliable source.
It is a correct paraphrase because the wording is different enough that the website does not need to be named.
It is plagiarism because you named the idea but failed to copy it word for word enough to count as a real quote.
It is plagiarism because the exact words belong to the website, and removing the quotation marks does not make them yours.
hints: The lesson says that taking off quotation marks does not turn a borrowed idea into the student's own — what rule does that break?
When words are the source's exact words, what signal must a reader see to know they are not the student's own?

problemText: A nutrition guide for kids says: 'Eating vegetables that are different colors gives your body a wider range of vitamins and minerals.' You decide the exact wording is not important for your health project — the general idea is enough. You write: 'Different colored vegetables give the body a wider range of vitamins and minerals.' Is this a correct paraphrase of the source? Explain why or why not.
choices: No, because the sentence order and structure are identical to the source, with only a few words swapped — that is a word swap, not a real paraphrase.
Yes, because you changed some of the words like 'eating' to 'different colored' and 'your body' to 'the body,' so it counts as a real paraphrase.
Yes, because you included the source's main idea about vitamins and minerals and explained it in a way your reader will understand clearly.
No, because you forgot to use quotation marks around the part about the vitamins and minerals that came from the guide.
hints: Look at where the main parts sit in both sentences — do they stay in the same slots or move to new ones?
The lesson calls this mistake 'a copy in a costume' — what is the trap that catches most students?

problemText: You are writing a report about tornadoes and you find this sentence: 'Tornadoes spin so fast that their winds can tear trees out of the ground and demolish buildings.' You use the look-away method to paraphrase it. You read the sentence, look away, and say out loud: 'When a tornado spins, the wind moves so hard that it can destroy trees and knock down houses.' You write this down. Then you look back to check accuracy. Did the look-away method work correctly? What is your next step?
choices: No, the look-away method failed because your paraphrase is shorter than the original sentence, so you left out important details.
Yes, the look-away method worked — your paraphrase got the idea right and changed the sentence structure, so you should now name the source when you use this sentence in your report.
No, the look-away method did not work because you still used some of the source's exact words, like 'tornado,' 'wind,' and 'buildings.'
Yes, the look-away method worked, but you need to go back and make your paraphrase longer to match the original exactly.
hints: The look-away method checks that you got the idea right and rebuilt the sentence shape — did you do both of those things?
What is the final reason the lesson gives for looking back at the source — to check accuracy or to borrow its sentence shape?

problemText: A bird encyclopedia states: 'Hummingbirds have the fastest heartbeats of any bird, which can reach 1,200 beats per minute.' In your report, you write: 'A hummingbird's heart beats at speeds of up to 1,200 times per minute, making it the fastest of all birds.' You also write: 'According to the bird encyclopedia, hummingbirds have the fastest heartbeats of any bird, which can reach 1,200 beats per minute.' Both sentences are now in your report, and you have named the encyclopedia twice. Is this correct? Why or why not?
choices: Yes, it is correct because you named the source twice, so the reader will know both ideas came from the encyclopedia and you did not steal them.
No, because the first paraphrase needs quotation marks around the part about the 1,200 beats per minute since that exact number came from the source.
No, because the second sentence copies the source's exact words and needs quotation marks around the copied part, while the first sentence is a real paraphrase and does not.
Yes, it is correct because one sentence is a paraphrase and one is a quote, and naming the source twice makes it clear you did not plagiarize anything.
hints: Look at the second sentence word by word — are those the encyclopedia's exact words or words you rebuilt?
The lesson says quotation marks are the only signal a reader has that exact wording is not the student's own — which sentence is missing them?

problemText: What are the three pieces of information that must go into a basic source record? Name them in order.
choices: AUTHOR (person quoted), SUBJECT (main idea), SOURCE (the website or book)
TOPIC (what the source is about), TITLE (the exact name), LOCATION (the place name)
WHO (who made it), WHAT (what it is called), WHERE (where it was found)
NAME (of the writer), DESCRIPTION (of the content), LINK (to find it online)
hints: The lesson uses WHO, WHAT, and WHERE as the three labels for the pieces.
WHO refers to the person or group who made the source, not someone quoted inside it.

problemText: A student finds a book titled 'Dinosaurs of the Jurassic Period' written by Maria Santos. She writes down: 'WHAT: dinosaurs.' Why is this incomplete or incorrect for the source record?
choices: She used the word 'dinosaurs' instead of 'Jurassic Period' in her notes.
She did not include the author's name anywhere in the record.
She forgot to write down where the book can be found.
She wrote the topic of the book instead of its exact title printed on the cover.
hints: The lesson warns about mixing up the topic (what a source is about) with the title (what it is called).
The exact title 'Dinosaurs of the Jurassic Period' is printed on the source itself.

problemText: A student watches a documentary video called 'Life in the Ocean Deep' posted on a channel named National Geographic Kids. In the video, a marine biologist named Dr. James Wu describes different deep-sea creatures. If the student is writing the WHO piece of the source record, which should go there?
choices: National Geographic Kids, because that is the channel that made and posted the video.
Dr. James Wu, because he is the expert speaking in the video and appears as the main source of information.
Life in the Ocean Deep, because that is the title of the video and describes what the source is about.
A marine biologist, because that is the professional role and job description of the person featured in it.
hints: WHO is not the person who is quoted or featured inside the source.
The lesson notes that a video can feature a guest speaking, but the maker of the source is the channel that posted it.

problemText: A student's incomplete source record reads: WHAT: 'How Maple Trees Make Syrup.' FOUND: National Geographic Kids. The article was written by Patricia Lin and appeared in that online magazine. Write out what the complete basic source record should look like, with all three pieces labeled and correct.
choices: WHO: National Geographic Kids. WHAT: How maple syrup is made. WHERE: Patricia Lin's article.
WHO: Patricia Lin. WHAT: 'How Maple Trees Make Syrup.' WHERE: National Geographic Kids.
WHO: How Maple Trees Make Syrup. WHAT: Patricia Lin. WHERE: National Geographic Kids.
WHO: Patricia Lin and National Geographic Kids. WHAT: 'Maple Trees.' WHERE: National Geographic Kids website.
hints: The WHO piece should list the person or group responsible for making the source, not what the source is about.
The exact title from the source goes in the WHAT piece, and the place holding the source goes in the WHERE piece.

problemText: A student takes notes while reading a magazine article titled 'Why Bees Are Important' by Soren Kim in Scientific American magazine. She writes: WHO: the scientist interviewed. WHAT: bees. WHERE: Scientific American. Which two pieces of her record are wrong, and why?
choices: WHERE is wrong because the magazine name itself should go there rather than just the publication type; WHO is wrong because the author Soren Kim wrote the article, not an interviewed scientist.
WHO is wrong because the magazine name should go there instead; WHAT is wrong because the magazine is more important than the bees.
WHAT is wrong because 'bees' is the topic, not the title; WHO is wrong because 'the scientist interviewed' is not the same as who made the source.
WHAT is wrong because she needs to name the magazine instead of the topic; WHERE is wrong because she should list the page number.
hints: The lesson teaches that the topic (what a source is about) is not the same as the title (what it is called).
The person who wrote the article is not the same as a scientist the article may have interviewed.

problemText: A student watches a YouTube video called 'The History of Basketball' posted by a sports education channel named Court Vision Academy. Inside the video, a retired basketball coach named Frank Rodriguez talks about how the game started. The student writes down her source record right away and correctly includes all three pieces. Later, she realizes she also wants to note that Frank Rodriguez is the coach who speaks in the video. Where in her source record should this detail go, and why?
choices: In the WHO piece, replacing 'Court Vision Academy' with Frank Rodriguez's name, because he is the main person in the video.
In the WHAT piece, adding 'with Frank Rodriguez' to the title, because he is part of what the video shows.
Separate from the three main pieces, as extra information about who is quoted, because Frank Rodriguez made the video but is not the person who posted it.
Separate from the three main pieces, as extra information about who is quoted, because Frank Rodriguez is featured but did not make or post the source.
hints: A source record has three pieces: WHO (maker), WHAT (title), and WHERE (location). Any detail that does not fit those three pieces goes elsewhere.
The lesson teaches that a person quoted or featured inside a source is not the same as the person or group who made it.
